title: Kirana and the Mangrove Map
blurb: An old tin box, a hand-drawn map and a rising tide. Kirana follows her grandfather's secret path into the mangrove forest.

chapters.title: The Tin Box
chapters.text:
When the school holidays began, Kirana travelled with her brother Bima to their grandfather's village on the north coast of Java. Opa's house stood on stilts, only a few steps from the sea. At high tide, the water licked the bottom of the wooden ladder. At night, Kirana could hear it moving under the floorboards, as if the whole house were breathing.

Opa was a quiet man with hands as rough as old rope. He mended nets on the porch and did not ask many questions. Their parents had told them that he had fished all his life, and that was all they knew about him.

On the second rainy afternoon, Opa asked the children to tidy the storeroom. It was dark in there, and it smelled of salt and tar. They found a rusty anchor, a broken radio and a bucket full of floats. Bima wanted to see if the radio still worked. Behind a pile of fishing nets, Kirana found a dented biscuit tin. It had been sealed with tape so old that it came away in flakes. Inside, wrapped in plastic, lay a yellowing sheet of paper.

"It is a map," whispered Bima.

The lines were drawn in blue pencil. There was a wavy coast, little pictures of trees, a tiny boat, and a cross in red ink at the far edge. Kirana guessed that a child had drawn it, because the trees all looked like broccoli. But it was a careful child. Along one thin line, the child had written the number of steps: two hundred.

"Treasure," said Bima at once. "It has a cross. Crosses always mean treasure."

Kirana turned the paper over. On the back, in shaky handwriting, someone had written: Follow the tide, not the path.

She read it twice while the rain drummed on the roof. How could anyone follow a tide? As far as she knew, it only went in and out.

chapters.title: What Opa Remembered
chapters.text:
At dinner, Kirana placed the map on the table, between the rice and the fried fish. Opa stopped chewing. He wiped his fingers, put on his glasses and said nothing for a long time. A moth bumped against the lamp. Bima kicked Kirana under the table. Then Opa smiled, and his eyes shone.

"I drew this when I was twelve," he said. "My father had come from Bali to build boats here, so we were the new family. In those days the sea was angry. The waves had eaten the beach and knocked down half of our houses. The fishermen said the sea took one metre of land every year. My mother put a stick in the sand to mark the edge of the water. Each year, she moved it further back."

"What is the cross?" asked Bima. "Is it treasure?"

"That is where I planted my first mangrove seedling," said Opa.

Bima's face fell.

"The old mangrove forest had been cut down for firewood and fish ponds," Opa went on. "That was why the sea could come so far in. An old woman who sold salted fish told me that the roots would hold the soil and break the waves. She gave me a long green seedling, as thin as a pen, and she showed me how to push it into the mud. Everybody laughed at me. A boy with a stick, they said, against the whole sea. I planted it anyway. The next day, I planted another."

Kirana's heart began to race. "Is it still there?" she asked.

Opa took off his glasses and folded them slowly. "I have not been back for years," he said. "My knees are too old for that mud, and the path is gone. Only the tide knows the way."

He tapped the back of the map with one finger, and he looked at them over the rice. It was hard to tell if he was asking them a question. Kirana looked at Bima, and Bima looked at Kirana.

chapters.title: Reading the Tide
chapters.text:
The next morning, Opa showed the children the tide table pinned on his wall. It was a long sheet of tiny numbers, and it listed the times of high and low water for each day.

"The sea rises and falls, pulled by the moon," he explained. "At high tide, the mangrove forest is half under water. At low tide, the mud appears, and you can walk between the roots. You may go in while the water is low, but you must be out before it comes back."

Kirana ran her finger along the row for that day. "Low tide is at ten o'clock today," she said. "High tide is at four o'clock." She counted on her fingers. "So it takes six hours to come all the way back."

"Very good," said Opa. "But you must not wait until four o'clock. The water does not rise evenly. It comes slowly at first, and then much faster in the middle hours. And it does not only come from in front of you. It runs up the creeks and gets behind you. By one o'clock, the creeks are filling. By two, you will not find your way back on foot. That gives you only a short time."

He went to the shelf. "I will lend you my boots. They are too big, so stuff the toes with rags. Take a rope, a water bottle and a whistle. If you are in trouble, blow three long blasts, and keep on blowing. And promise me you will turn back at the first sign of the tide."

Bima promised at once. Kirana looked at the back of the map again. "How can we follow the tide," she asked, "if it has gone out?"

"The water leaves a trail when it goes," said Opa, and he would say no more. He went back to his nets. But as she packed her bag, Kirana saw him take his old binoculars down from the shelf and wipe the glass with his shirt.

chapters.title: Into the Roots
chapters.text:
At ten o'clock, the children set off. The sea had gone far away, and the beach was a great grey plain of mud. Bima held the map and Kirana led. Their boots made loud, sucking sounds. With every step, the mud tried to keep them. Bima's left boot came off twice, and each time he stood on one leg like a heron and shouted until Kirana came back. Crossing the mud took nearly an hour.

At the edge of the forest, the mangrove roots rose out of the mud like hundreds of arched legs. Under the trees, the light turned green. All around them, the mud clicked and popped.

"They look like spiders," shivered Bima.

"They are called prop roots," said Kirana. "I read about them. They help the tree stand in soft mud and take in air."

She put her hand on one. It was wet and rough, and tiny shells were stuck along it. Then she saw a dark line on the trunk behind it, where the shells stopped. The line was higher than her head. She stopped smiling and looked at her watch.

Little crabs scuttled away, each one waving a single big claw. Small fish with bulging eyes, called mudskippers, jumped across the mud on their fins. Kirana laughed in spite of herself. "They are fish that walk!"

"How can they breathe up here?" asked Bima.

"They carry water in their gills, and they can take in air through their wet skin," she said.

The map said to follow the smallest creek for two hundred steps. They found it between two huge roots, no wider than a door. Some of the steps meant climbing, and some meant wading. They counted aloud together, one, two, three, all the way to the end. In that green, clicking place, the sound of their own voices was a great comfort.

At two hundred, they stopped. Neither of them was talking now. Kirana's watch said it was already past twelve.

The mud pulled at their boots, and Bima's boot came off twice
The children kept stopping to look for treasure on the way

chapters.title: The Wrong Turn
chapters.text:
After two hundred steps, the creek split in two. The map showed only one line, but now there were two. Which one was right?

"We should go left," said Bima. "It looks wider." He was already moving. "Wide means it goes somewhere."

Kirana caught his sleeve. She was not sure. Creeks could change in all those years. Then she remembered the words on the back. Follow the tide, not the path. And she remembered what Opa had said about the trail.

She crouched down and dipped her finger in the water. She felt a gentle current in the right-hand creek, flowing towards her and out to sea. Then she dropped a leaf into the left-hand creek. It sat there, turning slowly. The left-hand creek was almost still.

"At low tide, water drains out of the forest," she said. "A creek with a current comes from deep inside, where the water has gathered. Opa drew that one. It may look small, but it is the real way in. We go right!"

Bima grumbled, but he followed. "If we end up in a swamp," he said, "I will tell Opa it was your idea."

The right-hand creek was so narrow that they had to walk in it, with roots brushing both their shoulders. The mud grew deeper. They could not hear the sea any more. Mosquitoes whined around their ears. Kirana began to wonder if she had been wrong, but she did not say so. She just kept walking, and she kept her voice cheerful when she answered him.

At long last, the trees opened, and the creek led them to a small clearing with the sky above it. They had arrived!

But Kirana's watch said one o'clock. She looked down. A small leaf floated past her boot, and it was going the wrong way, into the forest. The tide had turned, and brown water had already begun to creep around their boots.

Bima had dropped the map into the creek

questions.prompt: Why did Kirana think the creek with a current was the right one?
options: It was the only one of the two creeks that was wide enough
It must come from deep inside the forest, where the water gathers
It was closer to the sea, so it would be safer for them
Its water was cleaner and looked much better to drink

questions.prompt: What does "Follow the tide, not the path" turn out to mean?
options: Use the flow of the water, because the shape of a path can mislead you
Walk only at night, when the water is high and the moon is out
Keep the sea on your left side and do not look at the map
Stay away from the water and wait for the tide to go right out
questions.why: Bima's creek looks like a path because it is wide. Kirana ignores how it looks and uses the current, and that leads them to the clearing.

questions.prompt: Why did Kirana not tell Bima that she was starting to worry?
options: She wanted him to get lost in the mangrove forest
She did not want to frighten him or make him turn back
She was too tired from the walk to say anything
She had already forgotten what she had told him
questions.why: She begins to wonder if she was wrong, but she keeps her voice cheerful. She is the one leading, so she is keeping him calm.

questions.prompt: How did Kirana notice that the tide had turned?
options: Bima's boot came off again and started to sink
The mudskippers all jumped into the creek at once
A wave broke over the tops of the mangrove trees
A small leaf floated into the forest instead of out
questions.why: A small leaf floated past her boot, and it was going the wrong way, into the forest.

questions.prompt: Why is one o'clock a worrying time for the children?
options: The batteries in Kirana's old watch were about to run out
The mosquitoes in the forest always come out at that time
Opa said the creeks start to fill by then, and they are far from home
They had promised to be home for their lunch at noon
questions.why: Opa warned them, "By one o'clock, the creeks are filling." Now they are deep in the forest and the water is rising.

chapters.title: The First Tree
chapters.text:
In the clearing stood a mangrove tree taller than their house. Its trunk was thick and grey, and its branches spread wide. Around it, hundreds of younger trees grew in neat rows, one behind another. A wooden board, almost covered with moss, read: First tree, planted by Wayan, aged twelve.

"Opa was Wayan!" shouted Bima. "That is his name!" He had completely forgotten about treasure.

Kirana touched the rough bark. "He was right," she whispered. "He grew a whole forest."

She looked through the trees towards the sea. Somewhere out there, the waves were breaking on all these roots, long before they could reach the village. Above her head hung long green seedlings, as thin as pens. She reached up and took one.

"Kirana," said Bima in a small voice. "The water."

It had reached the tops of their boots. The creek they had come by was twice as wide now, and it was moving fast. They could never walk back that way.

Kirana made herself breathe slowly. She tied the rope around the old trunk and helped Bima up onto the lowest branch. Then she climbed up beside him and blew her whistle three long blasts, as Opa had asked. She counted to ten, and she blew again. The sound travelled over the water.

Soon the engine of a small boat came closer, nosing up the creek on the rising tide. Opa was standing at the front. He had been watching from the sea wall with binoculars since ten o'clock. He lifted the children on board.

Then he turned off the engine, and nobody spoke. Opa looked at the tree with wet eyes and patted its trunk, the way you might pat an old buffalo.

"Thank you for finding my little friend," he said. "They all laughed at him once."

Kirana held out the green seedling. "Where should this one go?" she asked.

Opa began to smile. "How much of your holiday is left?" he said.

questions.prompt: How tall was the first tree?
options: Taller than their house
As tall as Bima
As tall as a sea wall
Only one metre tall
questions.why: In the clearing stood a mangrove tree taller than their house.

questions.prompt: What do the neat rows of younger trees suggest?
options: A big company had come to plant them for its timber
Someone planted them one by one over many years
The children had made a mistake about what they were
The trees had grown from seeds carried in by the sea
questions.why: Wild trees do not grow in neat rows. Opa said he planted another the next day, and Kirana says he grew a whole forest.

questions.prompt: What name was on the wooden board?
options: Kirana
Opa
Wayan
Bima
questions.why: The board read: First tree, planted by Wayan, aged twelve.

questions.prompt: How can you tell that Bima's feelings have changed?
options: He starts asking when they will get to the treasure
He says that the tree is much smaller than he hoped
He sits down and refuses to walk another step
He is excited about Opa's name and forgets about treasure
questions.why: He shouts with joy at Opa's name, and the text says he had completely forgotten about treasure.

questions.prompt: Why could the children not walk back?
options: The creek was wider, moving fast and full of rising water
The rope had been left behind in the clearing
Bima's left boot had been lost in the deep mud
A boat had blocked the narrow creek behind them
questions.why: The water reached the tops of their boots, and the creek was twice as wide and moving fast.

questions.prompt: What did Kirana do to call for help?
options: She lit a small fire on a branch
She sent Bima back to fetch Opa
She blew three long blasts on her whistle
She waved the map above her head
questions.why: She blew her whistle three long blasts, as Opa had asked, then counted to ten and blew again.

questions.prompt: How did Opa know that the children needed him?
options: The neighbour had seen them in the creek and told him
He had been watching with binoculars and heard the whistle
He had gone with them all the way through the forest
He had planned to meet them at the tree at one o'clock
questions.why: He had been watching from the sea wall with binoculars since ten o'clock. The whistle sound travelled over the water.

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the story?
options: Maps are always right if you follow them carefully
Treasure is something you can only find by accident
Children should never walk in mud without a grown-up
One small act of care can grow into something that protects others
questions.why: A boy's seedling, laughed at by the village, became a forest that breaks the waves before they reach the village.
